conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim is supported, citing randomized trial evidence showing reduced mother-to-child transmission and WHO guidelines recommending tenofovir starting in the third trimester for pregnant women with high HBV DNA.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is supported, not false—provided it means tenofovir *in addition to* standard infant immunoprophylaxis (hepatitis-B vaccine birth dose and usually HBIG), in mothers with high HBV DNA.

The key randomized trial enrolled 200 HBeAg-positive pregnant women with HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate begun at 30–32 weeks reduced infant infection: 0% versus 7% in the per-protocol comparison (all infants received immunoprophylaxis). The intention-to-treat figures were less clean because of missing infant outcome data, but also favored tenofovir (5% vs 18%). Thus it is direct evidence for the specified high-viral-load, late-pregnancy setting.  
http://www.corevih-bretagne.fr/ckfinder/userfiles/files/Congrès/CROI_2017/Articles_Mercredi_15/Pan+et+al_+-+2016+-+Tenofovir+to+Prevent+Hepatitis+B+Transmission+in+M.pdf

There is an important qualification: another placebo-controlled trial found very low transmission in both groups when neonatal prevention was delivered extremely effectively, so it did not show a statistically clear incremental benefit. This does not establish that tenofovir is ineffective; it shows that the absolute benefit depends on baseline “immunoprophylaxis failure” risk and delivery of infant prophylaxis.  
https://www.hepatitisb.uw.edu/pdf/prevention-hbv/preventing-perinatal-transmission-hbv/core-concept/all

WHO nevertheless recommends tenofovir from week 28 through at least delivery for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL, specifically to prevent mother-to-child transmission.  
https://www.aidsdatahub.org/sites/default/files/resource/who-pmtct-hepatitis-b-virus-2020.pdf

So, the defensible skeptical view is not “tenofovir does not reduce transmission,” but rather that its added benefit is context-dependent and it is an adjunct—not a substitute—for timely infant vaccination/HBIG.
